title: Turn one customer review into five posts
purpose: Get a week of social proof out of a single good review.

fields.name: business
fields.help: what you sell and who to

prompt:
You are helping a small business turn one customer review into social posts.

Review (use the customer's exact words, do not embellish):
{{review}}

Business: {{business}}
Platforms: {{platforms}}

Write five different posts based on this review:
1. A quote post that leads with the strongest line of the review.
2. A short story post: the customer's problem, what happened, the result.
3. A post that answers the doubt this review overcomes.
4. A behind-the-scenes post about the work that earned the review.
5. A thank-you post addressed to the customer (first name only, or "a customer" if no name is given).

Rules:
- Never invent details, numbers or results that are not in the review.
- Keep each post under 120 words and match the norms of each platform listed.
- End each with one plain call to action.
- After the posts, list any claim you were tempted to add but left out because the review did not support it.
example:
### Input used

**{{review}}**
~~~~
Brought in my daughter's old bike thinking it was a lost cause. Marcus (the owner) told me straight up what needed fixing and what could wait, didn't try to upsell me anything. Had it back to me in two days and the price was less than I was braced for. She's been riding it to school every day since. Will be back for my own bike in spring. Five stars. - Jen T.
~~~~

**{{business}}**
~~~~
Pine & Pivot Bike Repair, a two-person neighborhood bike shop in Duluth, Minnesota. We do tune-ups and repairs for everyday riders, commuters and families.
~~~~

**{{platforms}}**
~~~~
Instagram and Facebook
~~~~

### Output

~~~~
1. Quote post (Instagram + Facebook)
“Marcus (the owner) told me straight up what needed fixing and what could wait, didn't try to upsell me anything.”

Thank you, Jen T., for the five stars and for saying out loud what we most want to be known for.

Message us to book your bike in.

#BikeRepair #Duluth

2. Short story post (Instagram + Facebook)
Jen brought in her daughter's old bike thinking it was a lost cause.

We looked it over and told her what needed fixing and what could wait. She had it back in two days, and the price was less than she was braced for.

Her daughter has been riding it to school every day since.

Got an old bike in the garage? Message us and ask.

3. Answering the doubt (Facebook-first, works on Instagram)
"Is my old bike even worth fixing, or will the shop just try to sell me more?"

Jen brought her daughter's bike in "thinking it was a lost cause." What she got was a straight answer about what needed fixing, what could wait, and no upselling.

Wondering the same about yours? Message us and ask.

4. Behind-the-scenes post (Instagram + Facebook)
The work that earned this review, in Jen's words: Marcus "told me straight up what needed fixing and what could wait."

That is the job. Look at the bike, sort what needs doing now from what can wait, say so plainly, and don't push extras. Jen had her daughter's bike back in two days.

Bring us the bike you've been putting off. Message us to book a spot.

#BikeRepair #Duluth

5. Thank-you post to the customer (Instagram + Facebook)
Thank you, Jen!

You told us your daughter has been riding that old bike to school every day since you picked it up. That is about the best thing a bike shop can hear.

Thanks for trusting us with it, and for the five stars. We'll see you in spring for your own bike.

Message us when you're ready to book.

Claims I was tempted to add but left out because the review does not support them:
- What was actually wrong with the bike or which parts were replaced (the review only says it seemed like a lost cause).
- Any price, discount or the word "cheap" or "affordable" (the review only says the price was less than she braced for).
- That Marcus is certified, experienced or has been in business for any length of time.
- That every customer gets the same honest advice, or that the shop never upsells (that is Jen's experience, not a guarantee).
- That the bike now "rides like new" or is safe for kids (the review says only that she rides it to school every day).
- That the shop offers fast or two-day turnaround on every job (the review says two days for this bike).
- That Jen is a longtime customer (she says she will be back, not that she has been before).
~~~~

title: Hook rewriter: ten openers for one post
purpose: Fix a post that is good but starts slowly.
prompt:
Here is a draft post for {{platform}}:

{{post}}

Write ten alternative opening lines for it. Use a different approach for each: a specific number, a question, a mistake, a contrast, a short story opening, a bold claim the post supports, a "most people" framing, a result first, a direct address to the reader, and a plain statement.

Rules:
- Each opener must be true to what the post actually says. Do not promise something the post does not deliver.
- Keep each under 15 words.
- After the list, pick the two you would test first and explain why in one sentence each.
- Then show the full post rewritten with your first pick, changing as little else as possible.
example:
### Input used

**{{post}}**
~~~~
Last month a customer came in with 500 flyers she'd had printed online for her grand opening. The colors came out muddy and the text sat so close to the edge that half of it got trimmed off. She'd paid $140 and had to reorder with us.

Here's what I tell everyone now. Before you send any file to print, check three things.

First, set your file to CMYK, not RGB. Screens show colors that printers can't make.

Second, keep all text at least an eighth of an inch inside the trim line.

Third, ask for a physical proof, even if it costs $10 more.

These three checks take about 15 minutes and have saved our customers hundreds of dollars in reprints this year. If you're planning a print job, send me your file and I'll look it over for free.
~~~~

**{{platform}}**
~~~~
LinkedIn
~~~~

### Output

~~~~
TEN OPENERS

1. Specific number: Three 15-minute checks can save you from paying for a print job twice.
2. Question: Is your print file actually ready to send to the printer?
3. Mistake: A $140 print order she had to redo, and the mistake behind it.
4. Contrast: Her screen looked perfect. The printed flyers came out muddy and trimmed.
5. Short story opening: Last month a customer brought me 500 flyers with the text trimmed off.
6. Bold claim the post supports: The file you approve on screen is not the file the printer prints.
7. "Most people" framing: Most people trust their screen when they send a file to print.
8. Result first: Three checks, 15 minutes, hundreds saved in customer reprints this year.
9. Direct address: Planning a print job? Check these three things before you send the file.
10. Plain statement: Check three things in your file before you send it to print.

TWO TO TEST FIRST
- #1: it leads with the payoff and a small time cost, which suits a LinkedIn feed where readers decide in the first line whether the post is useful to them.
- #5: it opens on a concrete story, which tends to pull readers into the line break before the "see more" cut-off.

FULL POST WITH OPENER #1

First, set your file to CMYK, not RGB. Screens show colors that printers can't make.

Second, keep all text at least an eighth of an inch inside the trim line.

Third, ask for a physical proof, even if it costs $10 more.

These three checks take about 15 minutes and have saved our customers hundreds of dollars in reprints this year. If you're planning a print job, send me your file and I'll look it over for free.

title: Reel script from a single tip
purpose: Turn one useful tip into a short video you can film today.

fields.name: tip
fields.help: the one thing you want viewers to learn

prompt:
Write a short vertical video script that teaches one tip.

Tip: {{tip}}
Business: {{business}}
Target length: {{length}} seconds

Give me a table with columns: time, what I say, what is on screen, on-screen text.
Structure:
- 0 to 3 seconds: a hook that states the problem or the payoff.
- Middle: the tip in at most three steps, one sentence each.
- Last 3 seconds: one call to action.

Rules:
- Spoken words must fit the time at a natural pace, about 2.5 words per second.
- On-screen text is at most six words per line.
- Assume one person filming on a phone with no editing skills. No shots that need a second person.
- After the table, write the caption and list what I need to have ready before filming.
example:
### Input used

**{{tip}}**
~~~~
After you wash a cast iron pan, dry it on low heat, then wipe a thin layer of oil on while it's still warm. That stops rust and you almost never have to do a full re-season.
~~~~

**{{business}}**
~~~~
Ridgeback Iron Co. - I restore and sell vintage cast iron pans online and at weekend markets.
~~~~

**{{length}}**
~~~~
30
~~~~

### Output

~~~~
| Time | What I say | On screen | On-screen text |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0-3s | "Stop re-seasoning your cast iron." (5 words) | Close-up of a dull, spotty pan held in both hands, then set on the stove | Stop re-seasoning it |
| 3-10s | "Dry the pan on low heat until the water's gone." (10 words) | Pan on a burner on low; a little steam rises off the surface | Step 1: Dry on low heat |
| 10-17s | "Turn off the heat and add half a teaspoon of oil." (11 words) | Hand pours a small amount of oil into the warm pan | Step 2: Oil while warm |
| 17-27s | "Wipe it all over with a paper towel until it looks almost dry." (13 words) | Hand wipes the inside, sides and handle; end on a pan with an even dark sheen | Step 3: Wipe it thin |
| 27-30s | "Follow Ridgeback Iron for more cast iron tips." (8 words) | Pan sits on the counter next to a shelf of your restored pans | Follow for more tips |

Word count check: 5 + 10 + 11 + 13 + 8 = 47 spoken words, roughly 19 seconds of speech at 2.5 words per second. That leaves natural pauses for the visuals in a 30-second video, so you can speak slowly.

**Caption**
Rusty cast iron usually isn't a seasoning problem, it's a drying problem. Dry it on low heat, add a few drops of oil while it's still warm, wipe it thin, and you're done. Save this for the next time you wash your pan. #castiron #castironcare #cookingtips #kitchentips

**Have ready before filming**
- One cast iron pan, washed and ready to dry
- A stove burner you can set to low
- Cooking oil in a small cup or bottle, about half a teaspoon measured out
- A paper towel
- Your phone propped at chest height on a stack of books, pointing at the stove, so both hands are free
- A second, restored pan on a shelf or counter for the last shot
- Good daylight from a window, with the light on the pan and not behind it
~~~~

title: Shot list for a 30-second product demo
purpose: Know exactly what to film before you pick up the phone.

fields.name: product
fields.help: what it is and what it does

fields.name: key_benefit
fields.help: the one thing the viewer should remember

prompt:
Create a shot list for a 30-second product demo video.

Product: {{product}}
The one thing viewers should remember: {{key_benefit}}
Where I can film: {{setting}}

Give me a numbered list of six to eight shots. For each: duration, framing (wide, medium, close), what happens, and any on-screen text.

Rules:
- The first shot shows the product in use, not a logo.
- The key benefit must be shown, not only said.
- Include one close-up of a detail.
- Total duration adds up to 30 seconds. Show the sum.
- Phone camera, natural light, no special gear.
- End with a list of props to gather and the order to film in so I move the camera as little as possible.
example:
### Input used

**{{product}}**
~~~~
Fieldmouse Fold Bowl - a silicone collapsible dog water bowl. It holds 24 oz, folds flat to about 1 inch thick, has a carabiner clip, and is dishwasher safe.
~~~~

**{{key_benefit}}**
~~~~
It folds flat enough to fit in a jacket pocket.
~~~~

**{{setting}}**
~~~~
My front porch and the kitchen counter in my house. It's just me and my dog Biscuit, daylight from the porch and the kitchen window. I'll prop my phone on books.
~~~~

### Output

~~~~
**Shot list: 30-second demo of the Fieldmouse Fold Bowl**

1. **4 sec | Medium | Porch step.** Biscuit drinks from the open bowl, which is full of water and sitting on the step. Your hand rests on the rim. Text: "Water, anywhere"
2. **3 sec | Close | Porch step.** Close-up of the bowl's ribbed fold lines and the carabiner clip, with a drop of water running down the side. Text: "Silicone. Dishwasher safe."
3. **4 sec | Medium | Porch step.** Your hands tip out the water, then press the bowl flat in one motion until it is a disc. Text: "Press flat"

### Input used

**{{topic}}**

How to tell when sourdough dough is done proofing, so you stop guessing

**{{audience}}**

Home bakers who have tried sourdough two or three times, got dense loaves, and are close to giving up

**{{payoff}}**

They learn the poke test and the jiggle test, two quick checks for whether dough is ready to shape and bake

1. Question
   Spoken: Is your sourdough actually ready to bake?
   On-screen: Is it ready yet?
   Camera: Close-up, hands hovering over a bowl of risen dough, camera slightly above, you looking up into the lens.

2. Common mistake
   Spoken: Baking by the clock? That's the mistake.
   On-screen: Stop trusting the clock
   Camera: Phone timer in frame going off, hand silences it, then the camera pushes in on the dough bowl.

3. Number
   Spoken: Two quick tests tell you when to bake.
   On-screen: Two tests. No timer.
   Camera: Two fingers held up to the camera, then you point them at the dough.

4. Before-and-after
   Spoken: Before the poke test: brick. After: this.
   On-screen: Before and after
   Camera: Split screen: a dense, tight-crumb slice on the left, an open-crumb slice on the right, both held to camera.
   VERIFY BEFORE USING: Verify: only use this if you really have two loaves from the same recipe where the proofing check was the main change. Otherwise it implies more than the payoff, so cut it.

5. Stop doing this
   Spoken: Stop trusting the recipe's proofing time.
   On-screen: Stop trusting the timer
   Camera: A printed recipe with the proofing time circled; your hand crosses it out with a marker.

   Spoken: Doubled in size doesn't mean it's ready.
   On-screen: Doubled does not equal ready
   Camera: A clear tub of dough with a rubber band at the starting line, dough well past it; you shake your head.
   VERIFY BEFORE USING: Verify: "doubled" is a common recipe guideline but not reliable for every dough, flour or temperature. Back this up from a baking source you trust, or soften it to "Doubled doesn't always mean ready" before posting.

7. Result first
   Spoken: This dough is ready. Here's how I know.
   On-screen: Ready to shape
   Camera: Top-down on a bubbly, domed dough; a finger presses in and the dent springs back slowly.

8. Relatable moment
   Spoken: Sliced it open. Dense. Again.
   On-screen: Not again.
   Camera: Bread knife stuck halfway through a dense loaf, you glance at the camera and sigh.
   VERIFY BEFORE USING: Use only if it is true to your experience or you have a loaf to film.

9. Direct challenge
   Spoken: Try this before your next loaf.
   On-screen: Try this first
   Camera: You point straight into the lens, then point down at the dough.

   Spoken: (no speech)
   On-screen: Poke. Watch. Decide.
   Camera: Macro shot of a finger poking dough; the dent slowly fills in; the bowl gets a gentle wiggle and the dough jiggles.

1. Hook 8 (relatable moment): bakers who have given up on sourdough will recognize that sliced-open sigh instantly, which earns the next two seconds.
2. Hook 7 (result first): it shows the exact test the video teaches, so the viewer sees the payoff before deciding to stay.
3. Hook 3 (number): "two tests" is a concrete, small promise that fits discouraged bakers who want something simple.

prompt:
Plan a blog article.

Target keyword: {{keyword}}
Business: {{business}}
What I know first-hand: {{expertise}}

Give me:
1. The likely intent behind this search, and what the reader wants to be able to do after reading.
2. Three title options under 60 characters.
3. An outline with H2 and H3 headings. Under each heading, one line on what to cover and which of my first-hand points belongs there.
4. A direct two-sentence answer to the main question, to place near the top.
5. Four related questions to answer in an FAQ section.
6. One original element only I could add: a photo, a number from my own work, a short example.

example:
### Input used

**{{keyword}}**
~~~~
how to winterize a sprinkler system
~~~~

**{{business}}**
~~~~
Cedar Fork Irrigation, a three-person sprinkler installation and repair company serving homeowners in the suburbs of Boise, Idaho.
~~~~

**{{expertise}}**
~~~~
We do about 400 winterizations a season and have for six seasons. Biggest mistake we see: homeowners shut off the water but never open the drain valves, and the backflow preventer cracks. We blow out with a compressor, one zone at a time, at 50 psi max on PVC and 80 psi max on poly pipe. A cracked backflow preventer usually costs around $350 to replace; our winterization visit is $95. First hard frost here is usually late October and we are booked solid by Oct 20.
~~~~

### Output

~~~~
1. SEARCH INTENT

Intent: informational, how-to. The searcher is almost certainly a homeowner with an in-ground sprinkler system, searching in autumn, who is worried about freeze damage and unsure whether to do it themselves or pay someone.

After reading, they should be able to: decide whether DIY is realistic for them, shut off the water, drain and blow out every zone without damaging pipes, protect the backflow preventer and controller, and know when to call a pro.

2. TITLE OPTIONS (under 60 characters)

- How to Winterize a Sprinkler System, Step by Step (49)
- Winterize Your Sprinklers: DIY Blowout Guide (44)
- How to Winterize Sprinklers Before the First Freeze (51)

3. OUTLINE

H1: (use one of the titles above)

Intro (no heading): Lead with the direct answer from section 4, then one line on what is at stake (frozen water cracking pipes and valves).

H2: Why sprinkler systems need winterizing
Cover: water left in pipes expands when it freezes and splits the weakest parts first. First-hand point: the backflow preventer is what you see crack most often; you can set up the repair-vs-visit cost contrast later in the article.
Source needed: one general reference on freeze damage to irrigation components, such as a university extension office or a pipe/valve manufacturer guide.

H2: When to winterize
  H3: Timing in a cold-winter climate
  Cover: do it after the last watering and before the first hard freeze. First-hand point: first hard frost in your area is usually late October, and your schedule is full by Oct 20, so homeowners should book or start early.
  Source needed: your local average first-frost date from the National Weather Service or your state extension office. Do not give a date without it.
  H3: Signs you have waited too long
  Cover: overnight lows near freezing, water in the system you cannot drain. First-hand point: none supplied; add a short note on what you have seen on late callouts.

H2: DIY or hire a pro?
  H3: What you need to do it yourself
  Cover: a compressor and the right fittings, eye protection, your system's zone map. First-hand point: the pressure limits you use (50 psi max on PVC, 80 psi max on poly).
  Source needed: compressor volume (CFM) requirement. Take it from your own equipment or a manufacturer spec, not from memory.
  H3: When it makes sense to call someone
  Cover: unknown pipe type, no compressor, a system with a complicated backflow setup. First-hand point: your $95 winterization visit versus the cost of a repair.

H2: How to winterize a sprinkler system, step by step
  H3: Step 1: Shut off the water supply
  Cover: locate and close the main shutoff to the system. First-hand point: none supplied; a photo of a typical shutoff would help here.
  H3: Step 2: Open the drain valves
  Cover: relieve pressure and open manual drains so gravity clears low points. First-hand point: this is the step homeowners skip, and the one that leads to cracked backflow preventers.
  H3: Step 3: Blow out the lines, one zone at a time
  Cover: connect the compressor, run each zone until only mist comes out, and never run all zones at once. First-hand point: your 50 psi PVC and 80 psi poly limits, and why you work zone by zone.

2. Twelve questions grouped as: their situation, the problem and its cost, what they have tried, how they decide, and timing and budget. Order them so the easy ones come first.
3. For each question, what a strong answer and a weak answer would tell me.
4. Three signs this prospect is not a fit.
5. A closing that agrees a specific next step.

### Input used

**{{offer}}**
~~~~
Ledgerline Bookkeeping: cleanup of messy books plus monthly bookkeeping in QuickBooks Online for small trade and construction businesses. Fixed monthly fee, $450 to $900 depending on transaction volume.
~~~~

**{{prospect}}**
~~~~
Dana Whitfield, owner of Whitfield & Sons Roofing, a roofing company with about nine employees. Referred by her insurance agent. She told the agent her books are 'a mess' and her accountant keeps chasing her for reports in March. That is all I know.
~~~~

**{{call_length}}**

30

### Output

~~~~
DISCOVERY CALL PREP: Dana Whitfield, Whitfield & Sons Roofing, 30 minutes

1. OPENING LINE
"Thanks for making time, Dana. I'd like to spend the first part asking about how things work today, then tell you whether I can help, and leave us a clear next step. Sound okay?"

2. TWELVE QUESTIONS

A. Their situation
Q1. Can you walk me through how the business runs day to day, and where the money side fits in?
 Strong: a clear picture of who does what, and she knows where her numbers live. Weak: "it's all kind of in my head."
Q2. Who handles the bookkeeping right now, and what does a typical week of that look like?
 Strong: a named person or a clear routine. Weak: nobody owns it, or it only gets done when something is due.
Q3. What do you use today to track income and expenses?
 Strong: a tool she can name, ideally QuickBooks or something I can work from. Weak: paper, scattered spreadsheets, or no system.

B. The problem and its cost
Q4. What's been going on that makes the books a priority now?
 Strong: a specific trigger, like a tax deadline or a bad surprise. Weak: "I should probably deal with it."
Q5. When the books fall behind, what does that affect for you?
 Strong: she can name concrete effects such as cash decisions, taxes or the accountant's deadlines. Weak: she cannot name any consequence, which suggests low urgency.
Q6. What has it cost you so far, in time, money or stress?
 Strong: numbers or clear examples (late fees, hours, accountant overtime). Weak: shrugs, which suggests she may not feel the cost yet.

C. What they have tried
Q7. What have you tried so far to fix it?
 Strong: she has made real attempts, so she knows what she wants. Weak: nothing tried, or a history of starting and abandoning fixes.
Q8. What worked about those attempts and what did not?
 Strong: specific lessons that shape how I scope the work. Weak: blames people or tools without detail.

D. How they decide
Q9. Besides you, who else would have a say in a decision like this?
 Strong: she names the people (for example her accountant) so I can include them. Weak: a hidden decision-maker appears late.
Q10. How have you chosen outside help for the business before?
 Strong: a clear process she can repeat. Weak: no process, or a pattern of delaying decisions.

E. Timing and budget
Q11. What timeline do you have in mind for getting this sorted, and what is driving it?
 Strong: a date tied to a real event. Weak: "sometime this year."
Q12. How are you thinking about what to invest in fixing this?
 Strong: a number or range, or a clear sense of what it is worth. Weak: no idea, or an expectation far below the work needed.

3. SIGNS THIS PROSPECT IS NOT A FIT
- She will not share access to her bank and accounting records, which I need to do the work.
- She wants tax preparation, payroll or advice, which are outside what I sell. [Confirm against your own scope.]
- She expects the books fixed with no involvement at all, and will not answer questions or send receipts.

4. CLOSING (agree a specific next step)
"Based on what you've told me, a good next step is a short records review: I look at your last few months in the books and send you a fixed-price scope. Can we book [day and time] for that, and would you like your accountant included?"

5. TIME PLAN (30 minutes)
- 0:00 to 0:02: Opening and agenda
- 0:02 to 0:08: Situation (Q1 to Q3)
- 0:08 to 0:16: Problem and cost (Q4 to Q6)
- 0:16 to 0:20: What they have tried (Q7, Q8)
- 0:20 to 0:24: How they decide (Q9, Q10)
- 0:24 to 0:27: Timing and budget (Q11, Q12)
- 0:27 to 0:30: Closing and next step

If time runs short, drop Q3, Q8 and Q10 first.

- 0:02 to 0:08: Situation (Q1 to Q3)
- 0:08 to 0:16: Problem and cost (Q4 to Q6)
- 0:16 to 0:20: What they have tried (Q7, Q8)

- 0:24 to 0:27: Timing and budget (Q11, Q12)

fields.name: objections
fields.help: the five objections you hear most

prompt:
Help me respond to common objections.

What I sell: {{offer}}
The objections I hear most:
{{objections}}
Proof I can honestly cite: {{proof}}

For each objection give:
- What the buyer is probably worried about underneath.
- A clarifying question to ask before answering.
- A response under 60 words that acknowledges the concern, then addresses it.
- Which piece of my proof fits, if any.
- When the honest answer is "we may not be the right fit", and how to say that.

Rules:
- No pressure tactics, false scarcity or disparaging competitors.
- Use only the proof I provided. If none fits an objection, say so and suggest what proof I should collect.
example:
### Input used

**{{offer}}**
~~~~
Monthly bookkeeping plus quarterly tax estimates for solo contractors (electricians, plumbers, remodelers) with 0 to 3 employees. Flat $325 a month, run by my small firm, Ledgerline Books.
~~~~

**{{objections}}**
~~~~
1. "$325 a month is a lot, I can just keep a spreadsheet myself."
2. "I don't want to give my bank logins to someone I just met."
3. "My wife already does the books."
4. "I'm too busy to send you receipts and invoices every month."
5. "What if you get my taxes wrong?"
~~~~

**{{proof}}**
~~~~
- A client electrician went from five weeks behind on his books to books closed by the 10th of every month, for the last 14 months.
- Across the 14 clients who joined last year, our first-year catch-up work found an average of $2,100 per client in business expenses they had not been deducting.
- We prepared 31 returns in the last two filing seasons and none has drawn an IRS notice.
~~~~

### Output

~~~~
**Objection 1: "$325 a month is a lot, I can just keep a spreadsheet myself."**
- Underneath: Is this a cost or an investment? He fears paying for something he can do for free, and may not know what he is missing.
- Ask first: "What does your spreadsheet cover today, and when did you last reconcile it to the bank?"
- Response: Fair question. If you keep the spreadsheet current, you may be fine. Where clients have come out ahead is the expenses that slip through: across 14 clients last year, our catch-up work found an average of $2,100 each in expenses not yet deducted.
- Proof that fits: The $2,100 average in missed expenses from the 14 first-year clients.
- Honest "not the right fit": If his books are already current, his income is low enough that $325 a month outweighs any savings, and he is comfortable with the work, say: "It sounds like you have this covered. If it starts to slip, or tax time gets stressful, come back."

**Objection 2: "I don't want to give my bank logins to someone I just met."**
- Underneath: Fear of fraud or losing control of the money, and no basis yet to trust you.
- Ask first: "What would you need to see to feel comfortable, a read-only connection, uploads you control, or something else?"
- Response: That's a sensible worry. Here is exactly how access works with us: [describe your actual setup, e.g. read-only connections, who sees what, how to revoke]. You can start with a statement upload and decide on a connection later.
- Proof that fits: None of your three proof items addresses security. Collect: your actual access setup in writing, and a short quote from a current client on how they felt handing over access.
- Honest "not the right fit": If he will not share any financial data in any form, say: "Then we can't do the work properly, and I'd rather tell you that now than do a half job."

**Objection 3: "My wife already does the books."**
- Underneath: Loyalty and not wanting to imply she is doing a poor job; also not wanting to pay for something already covered.
- Ask first: "What parts does she handle, and which parts, if any, does she dread or find stressful?"
- Response: That's great that she's keeping on top of it. Some owners keep her in the loop and use us for the quarterly estimates and year-end, so it isn't all or nothing. Would a smaller scope be a better fit?
- Proof that fits: None directly. Collect: a story from a client whose spouse or relative kept the books before they joined, if one exists, and what changed.
- Honest "not the right fit": If she is handling the books and the quarterly estimates well, say: "Then you don't need us. If her time becomes the bottleneck, I'm here."

**Objection 4: "I'm too busy to send you receipts and invoices every month."**
- Underneath: He worries this adds work. He has probably already fallen behind and is a bit embarrassed.
- Ask first: "How do receipts and invoices get saved today, and how far behind are you?"
- Response: Understood, that's exactly when paperwork piles up. One client was five weeks behind when he started and has had his books closed by the 10th of every month for 14 months. We can agree a simple monthly routine up front.
- Proof that fits: The electrician who went from five weeks behind to closing by the 10th for 14 months.
- Honest "not the right fit": If he will not commit to even a minimal monthly routine, say: "Without a bit of input each month, I can't keep your books accurate, so this wouldn't serve you well."

**Objection 5: "What if you get my taxes wrong?"**
- Underneath: Fear of penalties, audit and being blamed; he wants to know who is accountable.
- Ask first: "Have you had a notice or a correction before, and what happened?"
- Response: A reasonable fear. We prepared 31 returns across the last two filing seasons, and none has drawn an IRS notice. I can also walk you through how each return gets reviewed before it's filed: [describe your review step].
- Proof that fits: 31 returns over two filing seasons with no IRS notices. Do not describe that as a guarantee.
- Honest "not the right fit": If he has complex issues outside your scope (for example multi-state payroll or an open audit), say: "That's beyond what we handle. You'd be better served by [type of specialist]."
~~~~

prompt:
Draft a reply to this customer.

Customer message:
{{message}}

What our policy allows: {{policy}}
Our voice: {{voice}}

First, in two lines: what the customer is asking for, and how they seem to feel.
Then write three replies:
A. Brief: under 60 words.
B. Standard: under 120 words.
C. Extra care: for a frustrated customer, under 150 words.

Rules:
- Answer the actual question in the first two sentences.
- Promise only what the policy above allows. If the policy does not cover this, say so and write the reply to hold the line while I check.

- List any information I need from the customer before sending.
example:
### Input used

**{{message}}**
~~~~
Hi, I dropped my commuter bike off Thursday for a basic tune up. The guy at the counter said it'd be ready Monday. It's now Wednesday and I haven't heard anything. I've been taking the bus all week and I really need the bike back. This is the second time I've had to chase you guys for an update. Can someone just tell me where it is? Jordan
~~~~

**{{policy}}**
~~~~
Standard tune-ups take 3 to 5 business days, and up to 7 in spring and summer. We text customers when a bike is ready. If we miss a quoted pickup date by more than 2 days, we take 10% off the repair. We cannot offer loaner bikes or cover transport costs. Pickups are Tuesday to Saturday, 9 to 5.
~~~~

**{{voice}}**
~~~~
Friendly, plain-spoken, a little dry humor. First names, short sentences, no corporate phrases.
~~~~

### Output

~~~~
**What they're asking and how they feel**
They want to know where their bike is, since it was promised for Monday and nobody has been in touch. They feel frustrated and let down, and this is their second time chasing us.

**A. Brief**
Hi Jordan, I can't see from here where your bike is, so I'm checking the bench right now. I'll text you by [TIME TODAY] with where it is and a pickup day. Sorry you've been on the bus all week. Could you reply with the phone number on your ticket? That helps.

[YOUR NAME], Camber & Chain

**B. Standard**
Hi Jordan, your bike was promised for Monday, and you shouldn't have had to chase us for an update. I can't tell you its exact spot yet, so I'm going to the bench now to find it.

I'll text you by [TIME TODAY] with its status and a pickup day. We're open Tuesday to Saturday, 9 to 5, if you'd like to come in. Could you reply with the phone number on your ticket and a quick description of the bike? That gets me to it faster.

[YOUR NAME], Camber & Chain

**C. Extra care**
Hi Jordan, I hear you. A week on the bus with your bike sitting in our shop is a bad deal, and getting no word since Monday makes it worse. I can't tell you exactly where it is yet, so I'm going to find it myself right now, not pass you along.

I'll text you by [TIME TODAY] with where it is and the day you can pick it up. I'll also tell the team to update you directly if that day moves. If you can reply with the phone number on your ticket and a quick description of the bike, I'll find it faster.

[YOUR NAME], Camber & Chain

**Notes before you send**
- Our policy does not say how to look up a bike's status, so all three replies are holding replies that commit only to finding out. Fill in [TIME TODAY] with a time you can keep.
- The 10% discount applies only when we miss the quoted date by more than 2 days. Wednesday is exactly 2 days past Monday, so it isn't triggered yet and I have not mentioned it. It will apply from tomorrow if the bike is still not ready.
- The policy does not cover loaner bikes or transport costs, so none are offered.

**Information to get from the customer**
- The phone number on the ticket (and the ticket or tag number if they have it)
- Their last name (we only have "Jordan")
- A short description of the bike
- The date and who they dropped it off with, if they remember

prompt:
Write a set of refund and return replies based on this policy.

Policy:
{{policy}}

Business: {{business}}

Write one reply for each case, each under 110 words:
1. Request is within policy: approve and explain what happens next.
2. Request is just outside the policy window.
3. Item is used or not in returnable condition.
4. Customer wants a refund but policy offers exchange or credit only.
5. Request needs more information before a decision.
6. A goodwill exception is being made.

Rules:
- Stay strictly within the policy text. If the policy is silent on a case, say so and write a neutral holding reply.
- State timelines and amounts only if the policy gives them. Otherwise use [TIMEFRAME].
- Firm where the answer is no, with one alternative offered where the policy allows.
- Finish with a list of gaps in my policy that these cases exposed.
example:
### Input used

**{{policy}}**
~~~~
Returns: 30 days from delivery date for unused, unburned candles in original packaging. Refund goes to the original payment method within 5 to 7 business days after we receive the item back. Customer pays return shipping unless the item arrived damaged or we sent the wrong item. Items bought on sale can be exchanged or taken as store credit, not refunded. Opened gift sets are not returnable. Damaged items: email a photo within 7 days of delivery and we replace or refund. Personalized candles are final sale.
~~~~

**{{business}}**
~~~~
Tidewater Candle Co. - handmade soy candles and gift sets sold through our own online shop.
~~~~

### Output

~~~~
**1. Within policy**

Hi [NAME], thanks for getting in touch. Your return is within our 30-day window, so we're happy to take it back.

Please send the candle back unused, unburned and in its original packaging. Once it reaches us, your refund goes to your original payment method within 5 to 7 business days. Return shipping is paid by you, unless the item arrived damaged or was the wrong one.

[RETURN ADDRESS AND HOW TO START A RETURN]

Reply here if anything is unclear.

Tidewater Candle Co.

**2. Just outside the window**
Note: Policy states the window but is silent on what happens after it, so no alternative is offered.

Hi [NAME], thanks for getting in touch, and I understand wanting a straight answer. Our returns window is 30 days from delivery. Your order arrived on [DELIVERY DATE], which puts it just past that window, so I can't accept the return or issue a refund.

I know that's not what you hoped to hear, and I appreciate you understanding. If anything else about your order doesn't look right, reply and tell me.

Tidewater Candle Co.

**3. Used or not returnable**
Note: Policy is silent on a candle that is lit and also defective; only the damaged/wrong-item route is mentioned.

Hi [NAME], thanks for telling us what happened. We accept returns only on candles that are unused, unburned and in their original packaging, so a candle that has been lit can't be returned or refunded.

If it arrived damaged or was the wrong item, email us a photo within 7 days of delivery and we'll replace or refund it. If neither applies, I'm not able to offer a return on this one.

Tidewater Candle Co.

**4. Refund wanted, policy allows exchange or credit only**

Hi [NAME], thanks for your message. The [ITEM] was bought on sale, and sale items can be exchanged or taken as store credit, but not refunded. So I can't return the money to your card.

I can do either of these: swap it for another item, or issue store credit within [TIMEFRAME]. Tell me which you'd like and I'll set it up. The candle should be unused and unburned, in its original packaging.

Tidewater Candle Co.

**5. More information needed**

Hi [NAME], thanks for writing. I want to give you the right answer, and I need a few details first.

Could you reply with your order number, the date it arrived, whether you're asking for a return, refund or exchange, and a photo if it arrived damaged or wrong? Damage photos need to reach us within 7 days of delivery.

Once I have those, I'll come back to you with a decision within [TIMEFRAME].

Tidewater Candle Co.

**6. Goodwill exception**
Note: Policy is silent on goodwill exceptions, so this reply is a neutral template with placeholders for what you decide.

Hi [NAME], thank you for your patience. Your request falls outside our standard policy, but we've decided to make an exception for you this time.

Here's what we'll do: [WHAT YOU ARE OFFERING: refund, credit or exchange]. Please [RETURN INSTRUCTIONS, IF ANY], and it will be processed within [TIMEFRAME].

This is a one-time exception, and our usual policy applies to future orders. Thank you for being a customer.

Tidewater Candle Co.

- No alternative is stated for returns after day 30 (store credit, a short grace period, or nothing).
- No process for starting a return: where to send it, whether you provide a label, who to contact.
- No store credit details: when it is issued, whether it expires, and whether it can be used on sale items.
- Unclear whether the 30-day window also applies to sale-item exchanges and credit.
- Nothing on a candle that is defective after burning (for example tunneling or a wick fault), as distinct from damaged on arrival.
- Nothing on goodwill exceptions: who can approve one, and what form it can take.
- Nothing on exchanges: who pays shipping, and what happens if the replacement is out of stock.
- Unclear whether original outbound shipping is refunded.
- No timeframe for how fast you respond to requests or damage photos.
- Nothing on partial refunds, for example a gift set returned with one candle missing.
~~~~

Rules:
- Keep the order of steps from the walkthrough unless a step clearly depends on a later one. If you reorder, say why.

**Standard Operating Procedure: End-of-Day Register Close-Out**

**Purpose**
To count the day's cash, match it to the day's sales report, and secure the money safely at closing.

**When to use it**
At the end of every day we are open, around 8:45 pm, after the last customer has left. Do not deposit at the bank on Sundays; the money stays in the safe until Monday.

**What you need before starting**
- The register and the Square terminal
- The clipboard with the cash log form
- A pen
- The bank bag
- The key to the cash drawer (it hangs on the hook)
- A printer connected to the terminal and paper in it
- A stapler
- [MISSING: the safe code or where it is kept. The walkthrough says a sticky note inside a cabinet, but the speaker wasn't sure]

**Steps**
1. Wipe down the counter. (I moved this step before the count: the walkthrough said it should happen before the count, even though it was mentioned later.)
2. Take the tip jar off the counter. [MISSING: where the tip jar goes overnight]
3. On the Square terminal, open the menu and go to Reports. [MISSING: the exact name of the end-of-day report option; the walkthrough says "end of day or whatever"]
4. Run the Z report.
5. Print the Z report.
6. Count the cash in the drawer once.
7. Count it a second time, to check.
8. Leave $200 in the drawer for the morning. [MISSING: which bills and coins make up the $200]
9. Put all the rest of the cash in the bank bag. [MISSING: whether the bag is sealed or labeled, and whether the cash needs to be in any order]
10. On the cash log, write the date.
11. On the cash log, write the total sales from the Z report.
12. On the cash log, write the cash you counted.
13. Sign the cash log.
14. Compare the counted cash to the sales total. If they are more than about five dollars apart, tell Renata. [MISSING: the exact amount, whether this means over, under or both, and how to reach Renata at night]
15. Staple the printed Z report to the cash log.
16. Put the bank bag in the safe in the back office.
17. Turn off the card reader. [MISSING: how it is turned off, and whether it needs to be unplugged]
18. Lock the cash drawer.
19. Hang the key on the hook.

**What "done" looks like**
The drawer is locked with $200 in it and the key is on the hook. The bank bag is in the safe. The cash log is filled in, signed, and has the printed Z report stapled to it. The card reader is off. The counter is wiped and the tip jar is put away.

**Common mistakes and how to avoid them**
- Miscounting the cash. Count twice, as the walkthrough says; someone got it wrong once.
- Splitting or paying out tips at close. Tips are split on Friday, not daily. [MISSING: where tips are kept until Friday]
- Forgetting to staple the Z report to the log. Do the stapling before you leave the counter.
- Depositing on a Sunday. Don't; leave it in the safe.
- Leaving the drawer unlocked or the key off the hook. Check both last.

**Who to ask when something is off**
Renata, the owner, for count differences. Marcus is the day manager and does the Monday bank run, so ask him about daytime questions. [MISSING: phone numbers or the preferred way to reach either of them]

**Questions for the person who gave the walkthrough**
1. What is the exact name of the end-of-day report in the Square menu?
2. Where is the safe code kept, and does it ever change?
3. What are the exact amounts for the $200 left in the drawer?
4. What counts as "off": is it five dollars over, under, or either? What should the person do if it is off by less than that?
5. Does the bank bag get sealed or labeled, and does it need a deposit slip?
6. Where does the tip jar go overnight, and who handles the Friday split?
7. Who does the bank run on Mondays, Renata or Marcus, and what time?
8. How do you turn off the card reader, and does anything else need turning off, such as lights, ovens or the door lock?
9. What should a new person do if the Z report won't print?
10. Are there other closing tasks that were left out, such as the front door?
~~~~

example:
### Input used

**{{offer}}**
~~~~
Mobile dog grooming: a fully equipped van that comes to the customer's driveway. Bath, haircut, nails, ears.
~~~~

**{{costs}}**
~~~~
Groomer pay $22 an hour. Time per groom: small dogs about 1 hour, medium about 1.5 hours, large about 2.5 hours. Supplies $9 per groom. Fuel and vehicle wear $6 per groom. Fixed costs $480 a month for the van payment and insurance.
~~~~

**{{current_price}}**
~~~~
$85 flat for every dog, regardless of size.
~~~~

**{{customers}}**
~~~~
About 60 repeat clients. Most book by text every 6 to 8 weeks and pay by card after the groom. Roughly a third small dogs, a third medium, a third large.
~~~~

### Output

~~~~
**First, your cost per groom (labor + supplies + fuel and wear)**
- Small (1 hr): 22 x 1 = $22, + $9 + $6 = **$37**
- Medium (1.5 hr): 22 x 1.5 = $33, + $9 + $6 = **$48**
- Large (2.5 hr): 22 x 2.5 = $55, + $9 + $6 = **$70**

At your current $85 flat price, the margin per groom is: small $85 - $37 = $48 (56.5%), medium $85 - $48 = $37 (43.5%), large $85 - $70 = $15 (17.6%). Blended across a third each: (48 + 37 + 15) / 3 = $33.33 per groom. The $480 monthly fixed cost is covered by 13 medium grooms (480 / 37 = 12.97).

**Option A: Flat price (what you do now)**
- How it works: one price for every dog. Keep $85, or adjust it for everyone.
- Who it favors: owners of large dogs, who get the most work for the same price; it is also the simplest to quote by text.
- Margin: as above. Large dogs return only $15 (15 / 85 = 17.6%) while small dogs return $48.
- What could go wrong: you are most busy with the jobs that earn the least. If your large dogs take more than 2.5 hours, the margin shrinks quickly.
- Track: actual groom time by dog size, and the number of large dog bookings per week.

**Option B: Tiered by dog size**
- How it works: set the price by size. As an illustration (not a market rate), choose prices that earn about the 43.5% margin that medium dogs earn now: small 37 / (1 - 0.435) = $65.5, so $65; medium $85; large 70 / (1 - 0.435) = $123.9, so $125.
- Who it favors: owners of small dogs (price drops $20) and you on large dogs (price rises $40).
- Margin: small $65 - $37 = $28 (43.1%); medium $85 - $48 = $37 (43.5%); large $125 - $70 = $55 (44.0%). Blended with a third each: (28 + 37 + 55) / 3 = $40.00, versus $33.33 flat, a gain of $6.67 per groom.
- What could go wrong: large-dog owners may leave or push back; small-dog price cut may reduce income if it does not bring more bookings. Dog size borderlines cause arguments.
- Track: rebooking rate by size tier, price pushback, and actual time per groom per tier.

**Option C: Prepaid bundle (a membership)**
- How it works: a client pays upfront for 4 grooms at a discount. Illustration for medium dogs: $300 for four, or $75 each rather than $85.
- Who it favors: your regulars, who already come back every 6 to 8 weeks; it favors you with cash upfront and locked-in repeat visits.
- Margin: revenue $300, cost 4 x $48 = $192, margin $108 (36.0%), $27 per groom versus $37 at $85.
- What could go wrong: you give up $10 per groom for a promise; clients may move, a dog may pass away or have a health issue, and you may owe refunds. It also does not fix the large dog problem unless sized.
- Track: bundle sign-ups, how many sessions get used, cancellations or refunds, and cash on hand from upfront payments.

**Comparison**

| | A: Flat $85 | B: Tiered 65/85/125 | C: Prepaid bundle (medium) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Margin per groom (S / M / L) | $48 / $37 / $15 | $28 / $37 / $55 | n/a / $27 / n/a |
| Blended margin (equal mix) | $33.33 | $40.00 | not comparable (medium only) |
| Simplicity | Highest | Medium | Medium |
| Cash timing | After each groom | After each groom | Upfront |
| Main risk | Large dogs lose money share | Pushback from large-dog owners | Discount without enough retention gain |

**What I would test first: B, on large dogs only**
Large dogs are where you earn least ($15, or 17.6%), so there is the most to gain and the test is narrow. Low-risk way to test:
1. For new large-dog clients only, quote $125 for the next four weeks.
2. For existing large-dog clients, tell them about the change on their next booking text, with a few weeks' notice.
3. Track acceptance rate, rebooking, and actual time per groom.
4. If most accept and rebook, extend to full tiers. If many leave, try $105 as a midpoint (70 / 105 gives a $35 margin, 33.3%).

**Market rates:** I can't see what other groomers charge. To find out, check the websites and social pages of local groomers, ask a few clients what they were paying before, and call two competitors as a customer for a quote by dog size.

This is a framework to help your decision, not financial advice.
~~~~
